articles.title: If You Need a Little Holiday Cheer, Nine Make-A-Wish Kids Are Just a Phone Call Away
articles.content:
Somewhere between untangling last year’s Christmas lights and realizing you somehow signed up to bring three sides to Thanksgiving, the festive spirit can start to feel a little MIA. Normally, we’d tell you to put your phone down and take a breather. This time, though, we’re asking you to pick it up.
Make-A-Wish has brought back its Holiday Wish Line, a number you can call for some old-fashioned seasonal cheer, courtesy of nine very special kids. Even if you’re a card-carrying member of the “please just text me” club, you might want to make an exception for this one.
First launched in December 2023, the Holiday Wish Line features prerecorded messages from children who have had their wishes granted by Make-A-Wish. Think jokes, holiday songs, personal stories and the kind of words of encouragement that somehow hit differently when they come from a kid.
This year, the hotline opened on Nov. 23, just in time for the Thanksgiving rush. Anyone nationwide can call (480) 914-9474 (WISH) through Dec. 31.
Before you dial, take a peek behind the scenes. Watching a group of Gen Alphas try to figure out a rotary phone might make you feel a little old, but it’s also the cutest thing you’ll see all week.
View this post on Instagram
This year’s lineup is part reunion and part debut. Seven of the nine have lent their voices to the hotline before, and two are brand-new. Every one of them has faced a major health battle and dreamed big anyway. Here’s how their wishes came true:
If listening to these kids leaves you a little misty-eyed (no judgment), you can help another child’s wish come true by donating at wish.org/wishline. You can also put those unused airline miles toward a dream trip or volunteer with your local chapter. And with Giving Tuesday landing on Dec. 1, there’s no better time to pay a little kindness forward.
You’d be joining a long tradition. It all started in 1980, when a Phoenix community came together for 7-year-old Chris Greicius, who was battling leukemia and wanted to be a police officer. Since then, the nonprofit has granted more than 650,000 wishes worldwide, and in the U.S., a new one is granted every 33 minutes.
The joy sticks around long after the day itself, too. In a 2022 survey of wish families, 95% of parents said their child’s emotional well-being improved, and just as many said the experience brought their family closer together. Not bad for something that starts with a kid saying, “I wish …”

articles.title: Here’s How to Easily Record Your Entire Family History So No One Forgets Who’s Who in All Those Photos
articles.content:
My sister and I were recently hanging out at her place, and the conversation turned to our childhood. I pulled up some old photos on my phone—snaps of pictures that used to live in albums at the center of my parents’ living room. We started taking guesses about when they were from and shared stories about what was happening in them. We both remembered family picnics at the waterfall, our dog Cujo (yes, Cujo), and flying kites in the cornfield across the house. But there were people, places and stories I couldn’t recall at all, like a close family friend’s house we spent a lot of time at; my sister could still describe it in detail.
That’s when it hit me: It had been years since we’d flipped through old albums like that. As physical albums get left behind and older relatives depart, we’re increasingly losing our family history.
I’ve researched bits of my family’s genealogy over the years, but I’ve always run into roadblocks. Like many families in the U.S., our ancestors immigrated several generations ago, and a lot of details were lost or changed along the way. How do you document family history when there are so many missing pieces? By tackling it little by little, says Allison Singleton, the genealogy services manager at the Genealogy Center. “There will be gaps of information you don’t know,” she says. But don’t let that stop you.
That being said, you’ll have a lot more luck if you have a method to the madness. That’s why I reached out to a few experts who do this for a living and could lay it out in simple terms for us. In addition to Singleton, I spoke with Kyle Betit, a senior genealogist at Ancestry; Haleh Shoa, a certified professional photo organizer and the founder of Picturli; and Peter Andrew Wint, the founder of Family Roots.
It turns out, there are a lot of strategies and resources available, and some of them are free. Read on to find out how to document family history, create a family tree and be the detective your clan needs—starting now!
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more family, holidays, humor, cleaning, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.
Before you dive into documenting your family’s history, determine your goal. “Knowing where you want to end up tells you where to start and how much you need to gather,” Shoa says.
Next, collect supplies. Shoa says you’ll need several plastic bins, colorful index cards for categorizing batches of photos, an archival pencil, a 2TB or 4TB external hard drive for storage, nitrile gloves for handling photos, and a notebook or spreadsheet for tracking.
Then, gather the documentation you already have and group it into categories. Think of this like taking an inventory. “Put like with like,” Shoa says. “The albums, the slides, the negatives and the VHS tapes should each have their own piles.” In addition to photos and videos, include things like old letters, newspaper clippings, obituaries, birth and death certificates, and recipe cards. “These items are full of clues about your family history,” Singleton notes. After you’ve grouped everything, you’ll dig into each category. (More on that below.)
Keep in mind that you don’t need to do everything at once. “Start small—with one photograph, one document, one family story, one person or one question—and see how your research progresses,” Singleton advises. After all, you don’t want to get overwhelmed before you even really start!
To create a family tree, gather and cross-check details about your family, and designate a place to keep it all organized. Follow these steps to get started.
Building your tree online allows you to save and share it virtually, and on some platforms, you can turn on collaborative permissions so relatives can contribute in real time.
If you’re looking for a free and simple platform that’s particularly good for beginners, Shoa recommends Family Echo. You can also create a basic free tree in FamilySearch, Canva, Ancestry and MyHeritage. Just be aware that free trees may have limitations, and access to some records and services may require a paid subscription.
Shoa offers an important note before you start: Businesses and technology can change, so wherever you build your family tree, make a habit of downloading a copy and saving it to your own computer, cloud storage or hard drive each time you update it.
All of the experts agree that you should start with what you know and build from there. “Enter your own name, birthdate and birthplace into the family tree, then branch outward to siblings, parents, grandparents and more,” Betit says.
As you start building your tree, you’ll likely discover gaps. Don’t get discouraged. “You are beginning your genealogy journey,” Singleton says. “The goal is to fill in those gaps.” Before you enlist outside or professional help, tap your relatives for basic info you might be missing.
“Once you’ve established your tree with information gathered by yourself or your family members,” Betit says, “the next step is to turn to research.” Ancestry has the largest paid collection, with more than 70 billion online records, including birth certificates, marriage records, census data, immigration documents, yearbooks, newspapers and more. Shoa notes that MyHeritage is also helpful if your family came from outside the U.S., particularly for those with a Jewish background. Other databases are out there too, and some of them, like FamilySearch, are free.
Also look into the free resources in your area. “Most public libraries offer genealogy databases for free,” Singleton says, and librarians can help you get started. If you hit a roadblock, Betit suggests checking local archives, courthouses, record offices, churches and cemeteries. If you’d rather not tackle this step yourself, you can hire a professional genealogist.
In some cases—like with Shoa’s family, who fled Iran due to the 1979 revolution—your family’s records may be missing. “Your relatives’ stories become the record,” she says, “so write them down.”
Once you’ve got the basics, it’s time to develop a more complete family history. “One way to fill in missing details, uncover stories and even correct misconceptions is talking with your living relatives,” Betit says. “Asking questions like ‘What do you remember about your parents or grandparents?’ can provide valuable context to help you on your journey.”
Speak to younger relatives too. “Family stories aren’t necessarily shared with everyone at once—they get passed along during everyday moments,” Singleton says. “Your cousin might have heard a story from your grandmother that you’ve never heard. Everyone has different memories and may hold another piece of the family story.” Show up to family gatherings (like upcoming holiday parties!) prepared. Bring photographs, ask questions and take notes or record what people share. You never know what someone might remember.
As you collect notes, stories and recordings, upload them to your tree and save them on your own hard drive or cloud storage.
Facing piles of photos spread across albums, boxes and drawers can be daunting. The best approach is to get organized, tackle a little at a time, digitize them and utilize a combination of technology and living relatives’ insights.
Shoa recommends starting with albums first. “An album is already in order, and the captions and the way the pages were laid out tell you things a loose print never will,” she explains. Take out the photos in the order they appear, batch each set by event and date, place an index card (with the date and event written on it) in front of the set, and line them up in the plastic bin (label bins by year or decade). Always check the back of each photo for info. If you want to add a note to the back, use a soft pencil and a light touch. When you finish all the albums, do the same for slides, negatives and loose photos.
After you’ve completed the first step, scan your photos at a high resolution (or hire a scanning service, like Picturli). Shoa recommends 600 ppi for prints and 4000 ppi for slides and negatives. Label each batch in the same way you did with the hard copies. If you’re hiring a scanning service, ask them to name batches according to your index cards.
When you get the originals and scanned copies back, it’s time to store them. “People often ask whether they should keep albums or go digital, and my answer is both,” Shoa says. “The digital copies are for sharing, and the originals are the heirloom.”
After double-checking that the digital copies match the originals, store the originals in archival boxes inside the house. If you want to put them back into albums, avoid albums with sticky pages and plastic film that can damage photos. And make sure to keep your photos out of attics, garages and basements, where they may be damaged by heat and humidity. For your digital files, Shoa recommends keeping three copies, with at least one stored outside of your home with a friend or relative.
Once you’ve digitized your photos, Shoa suggests using technology to help you identify who’s who. If you upload to Apple Photos or Google Photos and identify faces within the app (you can do this in the individual photo info), the apps can then find the same person across your whole library, she explains. MyHeritage and Ancestry also have tools that compare faces in your photos with family trees and historical records, but these work only with images of people who have passed.
Still unable to identify some faces? Share them in your family chat or bring them to your next gathering. “Set up a table with the photos, pencils and instructions for your family members to lightly write any identifying information on the back of the photographs,” Singleton suggests. This can prompt people to share more stories too.
You can also upload digital copies to your online family tree on Ancestry, Betit says. “Tag each person in the photo, and type up the names, dates, locations and stories alongside the image so that context is permanently preserved.”
Got a digital photo frame? I suggest adding some of your old photos to that. It’s a great conversation starter and another way to keep the stories alive when physical albums may no longer be lying around.
You’re bound to hit a few bumps in the road while figuring out how to document your family history, but the biggest mistake is waiting to get started. “We all think we’ll have time to sit down with Mom or Grandpa and go through the boxes,” Shoa says, “but then one day the only person who knew the people in the photos is gone. You can’t get that knowledge back.”
And it’s not just the information you could lose. “Waiting can cost you the photos too,” Shoa explains. Five of her clients lost their homes in the 2025 Palisades Fire in California. Everything was destroyed, but their photos weren’t; Shoa’s team had already scanned them and stored the copies elsewhere. “They were so grateful they hadn’t put it off,” she says.
Here are a few other common mistakes to avoid.
Make it a group project! Setting up a family message group and using collaborative family tree permissions so relatives can view, edit and add discoveries in real time can keep people motivated and engaged. Also give people real jobs. “A generic request to help with photos never gets done.” Shoa says. “But ‘Call Aunt Betty and ask her about the 1960s’ usually does.”
You can also schedule a monthly photo night or a video call where you share old pictures on screen and let everyone shout out names. And don’t count out kids! “Teenagers are great at recording their grandparents,” Shoa says, “and they ask questions the rest of us forgot to ask.”
If you get stuck, take a break or enlist help. You’ll have a fresh perspective when you pick back up, and “sometimes all it takes is learning about one new resource to get excited about your research again,” Singleton says. The Allen County Public Library Genealogy Center offers free weekly webinars, and the National Genealogical Society and the U.S. National Archives and Records Administration are also great resources.
And finally, while you’re staring at dates and names of ancestors you’ve never met, it’s easy to forget they were real people. If you have the opportunity, plan a trip to an ancestral hometown. “Heritage travel helps everyone feel a personal connection to the work and to your family’s history,” Betit says. “Walking the same streets your ancestors once walked transforms names and dates in your tree into something tangible, creating a lasting sense of identity.”
“We spend so much time trying to identify people in photographs from a hundred years ago that we forget to document the photographs we’re taking right now,” Singleton says. You probably have thousands of digital photos, but how many of them have names or explanations attached?
Our devices have become the modern “shoebox” full of photos, Shoa says. Don’t forget to gather those into one place (such as a shared online gallery or folder), the same way you’d gather the boxes from the garage, and add names, dates and details for future generations. You can also share and categorize photos, milestones and other living history on FamilyRoots. You might even want to print a few photos and curate a time capsule to be opened in the future.
“Our photos are the gateway to our memories, our past and most certainly our ancestors,” Shoa says. “When memories fade, and the paperwork is gone, they become the record.”
About the experts
At Reader’s Digest, we’re committed to producing high-quality content by writers with expertise and experience in their field in consultation with relevant, qualified experts. We rely on reputable primary sources, including government and professional organizations and academic institutions as well as our writers’ personal experiences where appropriate. For this piece on how to document family history, Sunny Fitzgerald tapped her experience as a longtime journalist who frequently writes about lifestyle, history and travel for Reader’s Digest. We verify all facts and data, back them with credible sourcing and revisit them over time to ensure they remain accurate and up to date. articles.title: How to Navigate Grief During the Holidays in Ways You’ll Actually Find Helpful
articles.content:
No matter what time of year you’ve lost someone, navigating that grief during the season devoted to joy, togetherness and sparkle can become a challenge unto itself. When my 82-year-old mom died the night before Thanksgiving three years ago, my grief became permanently imprinted into the holidays. Ever since, I’ve swung between wanting to eat cookies by the fire with Santa and scream through the streets with Krampus.
The holidays haven’t felt the same since, and admittedly, I even feel a little dread around this time of the year. I’m not alone. According to American Psychiatric Association’s Healthy Minds poll from 2025 about holiday-related concerns, nearly half of adults polled felt worry over grief and missing someone. The reality is that the best parts of the season can lead to some of the worst feelings of loss.
There is no easy answer here, unfortunately, but experts do have a few suggestions to help people handle grief during the holidays. For that advice, I spoke with Raman Mohabir, PhD, a licensed professional clinical counselor and the founder of Good Mourning Mental Health Counseling, and Tess Clarkson, an end-of-life doula and the creator of the Your Best Goodbye workshop.
Read on to find out how to get through the holidays after a loss, find special ways to honor your loved ones and maybe even enjoy the season again.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more holidays, relationships, etiquette, cleaning, travel and tech all week long.
First of all, it’s not your imagination: The holidays are harder. And the first notes of a familiar holiday song or the scent of a special dish can really feel like a gut punch. “The holiday season can further magnify grief because it is a time often marked with moments meant to be spent with family and loved ones, which can further highlight the absence of the person who has died,” Mohabir says. On top of that, you may feel guilt, anger or resentment for not feeling celebratory, and your grief can feel darker against all the sparkle.
How it hits can also depend on the kind of loss. Grief isn’t only about death, Mohabir notes. It can also include “ambiguous losses, such as the anticipatory grief associated with the decline of a loved one facing a terminal diagnosis, or loss due to divorce, deployment, incarceration or a miscarriage.” Those losses can be especially lonely during the holidays. “These ambiguous and disenfranchised grief experiences can complicate the holiday season as well, especially if the loss is not acknowledged or supported by others,” she says.
Whatever kind of loss you’re carrying, feeling as if you’re living a different holiday than everyone around you can be alienating.
It really depends on you. “There is no correct answer or moral obligation to how an individual should navigate the holiday season,” says Mohabir. A lot of it boils down to how you feel and who will be around you. Spending time with people who share your loss, or who are simply supportive, can be a real comfort and worth the effort. Spending it with people who aren’t supportive can do more harm than good, whether they’re friends or family.
“It is important to assess the quality of the support around you and what you need when gathering with others,” Mohabir says. Time alone counts too. “Choosing solitude and privacy can be restorative and healing as well,” she adds.
If celebrating feels like too much this year, try a gentler approach: “observing” the season or focusing on getting through it rather than celebrating it. “Maybe it is not putting up the tree or getting out the menorah,” Clarkson says. It’s also not all or nothing; Show up for dessert, pop by Christmas morning—”it’s about having more serenity without the performance of the holidays,” she says.
Start by listening to yourself rather than to your list of obligations. There’s no single right way to do the holidays while grieving. “It’s not a one-size-fits-all,” Clarkson says. “It behooves us to listen to ourselves for what we need.” That might be a walk, a good cry or a quiet night in, she says, or it might be more appointments with the therapist or a grief support group.
A little planning helps too, as long as you leave room to change course. Here’s where to start.
When dealing with grief during the holidays, Mohabir recommends the Hospice Foundation of America’s “3 Cs,” a framework developed by grief expert Kenneth J. Doka, PhD:
Before you arrive, decide how you’ll step away if you need to: taking a walk outside, spending a few minutes in a quiet room or driving yourself so you can leave early. Stepping away isn’t rude, and it isn’t giving up. “Self-care isn’t selfish,” says Clarkson. Even a few minutes alone to cry or catch your breath can help you rejoin the gathering and be more present. Don’t expect to be “all to everyone everywhere,” she adds.
People often say the wrong thing around someone who’s grieving—and sometimes, they don’t say anything at all. “As a culture, we don’t want to acknowledge this,” Clarkson says. “We’re obsessed with youth and living, and we turn away from anything that’s uncomfortable, so people don’t know how to behave.” Usually, she adds, “it’s not intentional. It’s just a lack of awareness.” It helps to have a response ready:
When grief hits mid-gathering, Clarkson, who is also a yoga teacher, turns to a simple grounding breath. Inhale “through the belly, blowing up like a giant balloon, counting to four,” she says. On the exhale, “imagine the breath going down to your feet, the floor and the core of the earth.” She likes five rounds but suggests doing what you can. Why it works: “Focusing on the inhale can help calm the swirl in your head.”
Grief lives in the body as well as the mind, and gentle movement can help release it. A walk around the block, some gentle stretching—anything to cause a shift in your body will help you feel better. Clarkson also suggests letting music do its job: “If you feel like dancing, don’t feel bad about it.”
Asking for help is hard when you’re grieving, so make it easy on yourself. When something triggers your grief, Clarkson suggests texting the friends you don’t have to explain anything to. Tell them what’s going on, then add something like, “I don’t have to say anything else—just know I need a little extra love.”
Support doesn’t have to come from a formal group either. A friend, a house of worship or your community can fill that role. “There can be support in a lot of different things,” Clarkson says, “not just formal support groups if that doesn’t feel right.”
Make room for them on purpose, whether that’s by keeping an old tradition, tweaking it or starting a new one. “You can make anything a ritual,” Clarkson says.
Sometimes the ritual makes itself. Every Thanksgiving and Christmas, when the stuffed artichokes came out, my Italian American grandmother would warn us in her deep Brooklyn accent: “Be careful—back in Brooklyn, Aunt Paulie almost choked to death on an artichoke when a pin from the choke got stuck in her throat!” After she was gone, my uncle took over the warning. Now, no matter which family members gather, or whether artichokes are even on the table, someone always asks, “Hmm, I can’t remember. There’s something about artichokes I need to be aware of, right?” prompting chuckles and someone stepping up to retell the tale of Aunt Paulie’s ordeal.
Here are a few ways to keep your loved one with you during the holidays:
They can. If you’ve just been through a loss, you know how much easier things are when you know what someone wanted, and a holiday table is a natural place to ask. One year after Mom’s death, my family started the conversation over Thanksgiving dessert. My dad laid out his funeral plans for us, and it turned into a lively, almost silly conversation, with the rest of us chiming in. “Death is a part of life, and we can’t run away from it or ignore it,” Clarkson says. “Or if we do, it’s going to complicate it.”
Talking about it now, while no one is in crisis, keeps the stress out of it. Clarkson suggests one simple question: What would be a good way to honor you if you weren’t here at this holiday meal next year? Many of the answers turn out to be joyful. “They might say: Make a toast, buy this bottle of wine, make these cookies, make this trifle, play this music, put up this one ornament,” she says. (Mine? Don’t cry for me, and please hire an Elvis impersonator.)
Asking now also means no one has to invent a ritual in the middle of their grief. “The more we talk about these hard things when we don’t need them,” Clarkson says, “the more we can create peace and be of help when it’s actually needed.” She recommends The Conversation Project for its free guides to help get the discussions going.
Often, the hardest part isn’t the holiday itself but the dread leading up to it. “Sometimes the anticipatory dread leading up to a significant date or holiday gathering can be exhausting and catch you by surprise,” says Mohabir. So don’t save all your coping for the day. “It is important to incorporate various restorative factors leading up to the expected trigger, rather than just focusing on coping with the holiday itself,” she says. Think: extra sleep, a lighter calendar, a walk or time with someone who gets it, all in the weeks before.
Timing can surprise you in another way too: The first holiday isn’t always the worst. In the first year, many people are still in shock, Clarkson explains. It’s often the second year, or even later, when the reality sets in. “Knowing that the holidays can create an uptick in the feelings of loss and grief can help you plan the care you’ll need for the season,” Clarkson says, “whether it’s your first holiday since the loss or your fifth.”
Whatever you feel this season, it’s allowed, whether it seems “right” or not. In fact, trying to bottle up holiday grief tends to backfire. “If we don’t deal with our emotions, they come out sideways,” Clarkson says.
Mohabir also recommends allowing yourself to experience moments of joy if they arise. “Grief is messy, and all reactions, including moments of happiness, are normal,” she explains.
After my mom died, I kept pointing out morbidly funny things that gave those closest to me (and myself!) uncontrollable giggles. That first Christmas without her, my nephew handed my dad, my brother and me light-up ugly Christmas sweaters, complete with words and gestures wildly inappropriate for the Lord’s birthday and what we had been going through. Donning our gay apparel while the Yule log crackled on the TV had us laughing so hard, tears rolled down our cheeks—a release we desperately needed. Laughing didn’t mean we missed her any less. “The range of grief reactions does not diminish the pain of grief or dishonor your loved one,” Mohabir says.
There’s also no deadline for any of this. Grief isn’t a ticking clock or a kitchen timer that dings when it’s done. “We don’t stop grieving. We don’t stop missing someone,” Clarkson says. “We learn to live with that loss in a different way.” It can still hit you years later, out of nowhere: “You might be missing somebody because you watch a commercial and it triggers that loss,” she says. So give yourself grace, “whether it’s the first holiday after a loss, the second, the third, the 10th, the 20th.”
You can also reach out for more support at any point, whether that’s a therapist, a grief group or simply a friend who will listen. It doesn’t have to happen right after the loss. “Sometimes it takes a team to help us in these shifts,” Clarkson says, “and that’s OK.”

You can also reach out for more support at any point, whether that’s a therapist, a grief group or simply a friend who will listen. It doesn’t have to happen right after the loss. “Sometimes it takes a team to help us in these shifts,” Clarkson says, “and that’s OK.”

Even the King of Rock and Roll couldn’t save a bad cocktail.

Priscilla Presley took fans on a trip down memory lane when she dug into her personal photo collection and shared a decades-old snapshot of herself and her late ex-husband, Elvis Presley, enjoying a night out in Hawaii.

The Instagram photo showed the two seated beside one another at a table. Elvis sported a blue button-down shirt with a scarf around his neck, while Priscilla wore a brown-and-black patterned blouse.

But perhaps the most entertaining part of the throwback is the story behind Priscilla’s less-than-enthusiastic facial expression.

Priscilla Presley revealed the hilarious story behind her throwback photo

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Priscilla Presley (@priscillapresley)

Priscilla explained what the couple—who were married from 1967 to 1973—had been doing when the picture was taken. “Elvis and I were watching Hawaiian dancers at an outdoor lounge,” she wrote, dating the photograph to sometime in the 1970s.

As for her expression? It turns out the evening’s refreshments weren’t quite to her liking. “That look on my face? let’s just say I wasn’t crazy about the drink I ordered!” she revealed, adding, “a priceless moment captured on film.”

The photograph struck a chord with fans, who flocked to the comments section to share their appreciation for the intimate glimpse into the couple’s relationship.

“Elvis is very much like his father Vernon in this pic – thank you for sharing it with us Priscilla ❤️,” one shared.

“I love it when you share your memories from the past every day, and I find myself looking forward to it more and more each day 🤎,” another wrote.

A third replied, “Love this photo❤️ very funny about your drink ! Thank you for sharing always.”

Hawaii was a special place for Elvis Presley

Long before the photograph was taken, Hawaii had become something of a second home for Elvis. According to Hawaii Magazine, the musician first visited the islands in 1957. He continued returning throughout his career as an escape and pace to unwind.

His fondness for Hawaii also became intertwined with his professional life. Elvis filmed three movies on the islands: Blue Hawaii (1961), Girls! Girls! Girls! (1962) and Paradise, Hawaiian Style (1966).

He also performed a benefit concert in 1961 that helped raise money for the construction of the USS Arizona Memorial at Pearl Harbor.

In 1973, just four years before his death at age 42, Elvis made television history with his satellite concert, Aloha from Hawaii.

Thanks for the throwback photo, Priscilla!
